newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FEATURE - Sarajevo's Anne Frank takes refuge in Ireland.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sarajevo's Anne Frank takes refuge in Ireland.

text.p: A Bosnian girl known as the Anne Frank of Sarajevo has found refuge in Dublin thanks to a diary of Yugoslavia's disintegration.
Zlata Filipovic lost her childhood, as did the young Frank, because of war.
But unlike Frank, who chronicled the German occupation of the Netherlands and died in a Nazi death camp, Zlata Filipovic lived to see her homeland taste peace.
Zlata's diary "A Child's Life In Sarajevo", published in 1994, proved a passport out of the city for her family, who continue to live off its proceeds.

The gravitas and clarity of the diaries caused some suspicions that they had been touched by adult hands but despite this the International Centre for Peace, in 1993, brought her story into the public domain and Zlata was offered a contract by a Paris publisher.
Hollywood's Universal Studios is reported to be adapting her diaries for the cinema.

The Republic of Ireland, with its 3.6 million population, did not question the authenticity of the diaries and treated the Filipovics in a similar fashion to most of the other 700 Bosnian refugees to whom it has given shelter.
ZLATA'S DIARY RECORDS WAR CHAOS

Zlata began her diaries when she was 10 and continued to write during former Yugoslavia's slide into chaos. She recorded candid accounts of the devastation of war and its impact on Sarajevo's innocent children.
A recent UNICEF report estimated that more than two million children, worldwide, have been killed in armed conflicts over the past 10 years, and in excess of six million seriously injured.
In former Yugoslavia the death toll is estimated at anything between 10,000 to 17,000, many of whom were children.
"It all started in April 1992 for me. Everything I had was taken away from me and my childhood was taken away because I had nothing to be a child about," Zlata said.
"I came home from school like I do here every day, I went out with my friends and watched TV and when I got up in the morning the war had started."

At first she said she was merely frightened but then she became angry at the injustice that was done to her and other children who knew nothing about politics but were robbed of their childhood by them.
"I was angry as to why this was happening. We were human beings. We had not done anything. We did not know politics. We were just children. We were innocent.

"And then I felt like screaming. Why was the world not doing anything to stop this and eventually I just became very sad. I was so very sad at what had happened. So many children's childhoods were taken away from them. For what?"
ZLATA AND FAMILY FLEE SARAJEVO, DIARY BUYS FREEDOM
Like other people in the battered city of Sarajevo, where Serbs and Moslems fought daily battles, the Filipovic family spent long hours trapped in a dark room afraid to go out.
They often had no fuel and candles were scarce but whenever she could Zlata communicated with her diary, talking to it as if it were a friend.
The family 'escaped' to Paris with the help of some high ranking officials after Zlata's diary made her famous.

They came to Ireland in October 1995 and now live in an apartment in Dublin's middle class south side. Zlata goes to an international school and is studying for the Baccalaureate which she will sit in 1998.
"We got out because of my diaries," said Zlata, "and now we live off the proceeds."
But although they are happy to have escaped, Zlata's mother Alicia said their lives are friendless and eternally sad.
"People want friends who are happy. We can never be happy. We have experienced things we cannot leave behind and we mourn and long for our home and friends in Sarajevo."
"We cannot be happy until we return to our home in Sarajevo, even then it can never be the same again," she said sadly.
IRELAND PROVIDES REFUGE
Her parents do not work and said they rarely leave their Dublin apartment.
"My father is a lawyer and even if he spoke all the languages in the world he could not get a job because he only knows Sarajevan law."
Zlata's mother, a research chemist who speaks hesitant English, also sees little chance of employment in a country where more than 11 percent of the population is out of work.
But they consider themselves lucky and Zlata said she feels so guilty to have managed to escape while others "who may deserve it much more" did not.
The Filipovic family say they have found a refuge but not a home.
